planting.note: Root semi-hardwood stem cuttings in shaded, humid nursery beds or plant established liners after the last frost against a stake or trellis; seed is rarely used since it loses viability within days of falling.

directions: Establish rooted cuttings in deep, humus-rich, consistently moist soil at the base of a tree, pole, or trellis, since this dioecious woody liana climbs by twining and will scramble many feet into a support if left unchecked. Eru is a slow-growing rainforest understory vine from Central and West Africa whose thick, glossy, leathery leaves are shredded fine and cooked into the beloved eru and okazi soups of Cameroon, Nigeria, and the Congo Basin, usually simmered with palm oil, meat or fish, and other greens. Because wild populations have been heavily overharvested, cultivating a few vines on a shaded fence or living trellis provides a sustainable home supply once the plant is established, after which stems can be selectively cut back for repeated leaf harvest for many years. Keep roots shaded and evenly moist and mulch heavily, as the plant resents drought and full, hot sun.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops & Plant Products
Kew Royal Botanic Gardens Plants of the World Online

common_name: Ashanti Pepper (West African Black Pepper, Uziza)

planting.note: Plant rooted stem cuttings in rich, well-drained soil at the base of a sturdy support after the last frost; this woody pepper-family vine climbs by clinging roots much like true black pepper and needs several years to reach fruiting size.

directions: Train cuttings up a post, tree trunk, or trellis in fertile, well-drained soil with light shade, especially while young; Ashanti pepper is a woody perennial climber native to the West and Central African rainforest that is prized for two distinct products from the same plant. The young, peppery-aromatic leaves, known as uziza leaf in Nigeria, are chopped fresh into pepper soups and stews, while the dried unripe fruit, uziza seed, is ground as a pungent, more intensely hot substitute for true black pepper. Harvest leaves lightly and repeatedly once the vine is established; fruit clusters ripen from green to red over several years as the plant matures. Mulch well and water during dry spells, since the species comes from consistently humid forest conditions.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops & Plant Products
Kew Royal Botanic Gardens Plants of the World Online

common_name: Negro Pepper (Grains of Selim, Ethiopian Pepper, Hwentia)

planting.note: Set out container-grown seedlings in spring into deep, moist, fertile soil in full sun to light shade; trees typically need 5-8 years before producing a useful pod harvest.

directions: Plant seedlings in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in a sheltered spot with full sun to partial shade, giving the tree ample room since it eventually reaches a slender, tall canopy form. Negro pepper is an aromatic evergreen tree native to the humid lowland forests and savanna transition zones of West and Central Africa, grown for its finger-like, slightly twisted seed pods that are sun-dried and often smoked before use. The dried pods and their small seeds carry a warm, smoky, camphor-and-pepper flavor used whole or ground in West African soups, stews, and spice blends, and are also valued in traditional medicine and smoked-fish preparation. Because it is slow to bear, most growers outside Africa treat it as a long-term agroforestry or specimen tree rather than a quick spice crop; young trees benefit from light shade and should be protected from strong wind while establishing.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops & Plant Products
Kew Royal Botanic Gardens Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Transplant container-grown seedlings into deep, rich, well-drained soil in a sunny to lightly shaded, wind-sheltered site; expect 5-9 years before the tree flowers and sets its first large fruit.

directions: Grow in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in a warm, humid, wind-protected location; African nutmeg is a mid-sized rainforest tree of West and Central Africa closely related to custard apple, notable for its unusual pendulous, ribbon-like, spiraling flowers followed by large round woody fruits the size of a grapefruit. Inside each fruit, numerous seeds embedded in aromatic pulp are dried and grated much like true nutmeg, imparting a similar warm, slightly bitter, musky-spicy flavor used in West African soups, rice dishes, and traditional remedies. Because seedlings take many years to reach bearing size, it is best suited to permanent agroforestry plantings or large tropical gardens rather than short-term cultivation, and young trees should be shaded and kept consistently moist during establishment.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops & Plant Products
Kew Royal Botanic Gardens Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Direct sow after the soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; young leaves can be picked as a cut-and-come-again crop within a month of sowing.

directions: Broadcast or row-sow seed directly into warm, well-drained soil once temperatures are reliably warm, then thin seedlings as young leaves are harvested. False sesame is a fast-growing annual widely gathered and cultivated across West and Southern Africa's savanna zones as a leafy relish vegetable; its tender, mucilaginous leaves are cooked much like okra to thicken soups and stews and are valued as a nutritious, drought-tolerant green in the dry season. The plant produces small tubular pink to lilac flowers similar to true sesame and its close relative, followed by seed capsules that yield an edible oil in some traditions, though leaf harvest is the primary use. Repeated cutting of the growing tips encourages bushy regrowth and extends the harvest window through the warm season.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops & Plant Products

planting.note: Direct sow into warm soil after frost danger has passed; broadcast thickly for a dense leaf-harvest stand or row-sow for repeated cut-and-come-again picking.

directions: Sow seed directly into warm, fertile soil after the last frost and keep evenly moist until germination, which is fast in hot weather. Bush okra is a fast-growing annual jute relative widely eaten across West Africa and Sudan, where the young leaves and shoots, known locally as krin krin, kraan kraan, or bush okra, are chopped and simmered into a slippery, okra-like soup base rich in vitamins and minerals. It is closely related to tossa jute (Corchorus olitorius) but tends to be more low-growing and branching, tolerating poorer soils and shorter, drier growing seasons. Harvest by pinching tender shoot tips every couple of weeks, which encourages continued branching and delays the onset of tough, fibrous stems and flowering.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops & Plant Products

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs or rooted sucker divisions in spring into moist to wet, acidic soil; established colonies can also be divided in early spring while dormant.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to light shade, spacing plants to allow the shrub's suckering habit to fill in as a loose colony over time. Steeplebush is a small native shrub of eastern North American wet meadows, bogs, and pond margins, prized by pollinator gardeners for its dense, fuzzy, upright spikes of tiny rose-pink flowers that bloom from mid to late summer when many other nectar sources have faded. The felted, gray-woolly undersides of the narrow leaves distinguish it from its white-flowered cousin meadowsweet, and the persistent dried flower spikes and reddish-brown stems add winter interest. It thrives in rain gardens, pond edges, and other consistently damp, sunny sites where few woody ornamentals perform well, and requires minimal pruning beyond removing old canes in late winter.
